Quant à l'attente, elle est comprise soit comme l'attente de la victoire promise au Prophète, soit comme l'attente du châtiment infligé aux incroyants. Al-Tabari retient que les incroyants demandaient quand viendrait «ce jugement» entre eux et les croyants, l'expression renvoyant au châtiment ou à la rétribution. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et al-Razi font écho à cette lecture, tandis qu'al-Kalbi et al-Farra' y voient la conquête de La Mecque, al-Sudi la bataille de Badr, et Mujahid et Qatada le Jour de la Résurrection. Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Atiyya rejettent l'interprétation de la conquête de La Mecque, car des Tulaqa' s'y convertirent. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Ashur rappellent que le mot «fath» désigne la victoire ou le jugement, et que la réponse divine évite de préciser le moment. Pour l'abrogation, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sam'ani et Ibn Juzayy estiment le verset abrogé par le verset du glaive, alors qu'al-Qurtubi juge qu'il ne l'est pas, le détournement pouvant coexister avec l'ordre de combattre. La lecture minoritaire d'Ibn al-Sumayfa' avec une fatha sur le dhad est expliquée par al-Farra' comme signifiant « attendu », c'est-à-dire attendre la perte de leurs adversaires, tandis qu'Abu Hatim préfère la kasra. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi concluent que le verset contient une menace voilée pour les incroyants et une promesse de victoire pour les croyants.
en: The commentators explain that the opening letters Alif, Lam, Mim belong to the disjointed letters whose meaning is uncertain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi leave it at saying that God alone knows what He means by them, while some later scholars, such as Ibn Uthaymin, read in them a challenge showing that the Quran is made of the same letters the Arabs use in speech. The following verses state that this Book is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, beyond all doubt. The polytheists claimed that Muhammad had invented it; God answers that it is the truth from his Lord, so that he may warn a people who had received no warner before him. Most agree that "no doubt" means there is no doubt about its divine origin. Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya explain that the Arabs had received no direct messenger before Muhammad, whereas Ibn Abbas and Muqatil place this in the interval between Jesus and Muhammad. The purpose of the warning is guidance, and "perhaps" expresses for some the Prophet's hope, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as expressing God's will. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan discuss whether "ma" is a negation or a relative pronoun, with grammatical consequences. Several commentators note that the surah was recited at the Friday dawn prayer and that reciting it carries great merit.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that the Qur'an is a revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds, beyond any doubt. Al-Tabari says it is neither poetry, nor the rhymed speech of soothsayers, nor something the Prophet ﷺ invented, answering those who claimed he had fabricated it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan hold that the pronoun in 'no doubt in it' refers to the whole statement rather than to the Book itself, and that the doubt is removed by the Qur'an's inimitability. Ibn 'Atiyya takes the denial as referring to the belief of the people of truth rather than the doubt of the disbelievers, while Ibn Juzayy relates it to the reality itself. On the phrase 'a people to whom no warner came before you', Qatada identifies them as the Arabs, an unlettered people with no earlier prophet, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil relate it to the interval between Jesus and Muhammad. Al-Razi argues that the Quraysh, descendants of Abraham, were reached by reason, and al-Zamakhshari holds that rational proofs suffice for knowing God but not for the legal rulings of the sharia. Most treat 'that they may be guided' as the Prophet's hope, though al-Zamakhshari reads it as an expression of desire. The commentators agree that the surah is Meccan, with a few exceptions named by some. The apparent meaning remains that the Qur'an is a truth from God, whose purpose is warning in the hope of guidance.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the claim of the polytheists that the Prophet ﷺ invented the Qur'an, and affirms that the Book is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, with no doubt about it. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, the word "bal" rejects this claim, and "am" here means "bal" with an interrogative sense of reproach or wonder. Most agree that the people addressed are Quraysh or the Arabs, who had received no warner before the Prophet ﷺ, and that the purpose of the revelation is warning and hope for guidance. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil relate the verse to the interval of no messengers (al-fatra) between Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the Arabs were held to account through reason regarding God and His oneness, though not through the revealed laws, which can only be known through messengers. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that Isma'il was sent to the Arabs before they abandoned his religion, and that the absence of a recent warner does not rule out earlier ones. Al-Razi argues that naming this people does not exclude the People of the Book, since the warning was more urgent for the polytheists. All agree that "la'alla" expresses hope, though al-Zamakhshari may read it as expressing desire, which Abu Hayyan criticizes as a Mu'tazili tendency. The verse thus establishes the divine origin of the Qur'an and explains its revelation by warning and the hope of guidance.

This verse states that God created the heavens, the earth and everything between them in six days, then established Himself on the Throne, and that besides Him people have neither protector nor intercessor. It calls them to reflect and remember. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the six days as days of this world, while al-Qurtubi stresses the perfection of creation and reports from Ibn Abbas that such a day equals a thousand years of worldly time. Al-Razi explains that the days stand for six states of beings, and that they are measured in human days because creation is an act that unfolds in time. On the Throne, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir affirm it as reported, without describing how, and Ibn Kathir understands istiwa as rising above; al-Razi and al-Nasafi understand it as sovereignty and dominion. On intercession, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya relate its denial to the disbelievers or to worldly intercession, and Ibn Juzayy notes that intercession for believers is only by God's permission. The commentators conclude that the purpose of the verse is to urge the listener to reflect and to affirm God's oneness.

The commentators explain that the verse means God directs the affairs of creation from the heaven to the earth, and that the matter then ascends back to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years by your reckoning. They differ on what this day and this ascent are. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and, in one transmission, Ibn Abbas, take it to be the descent and return of the command between heaven and earth, which are five hundred years apart, so the descent and ascent together make a thousand years covered by the angel in a single day. Al-Tabari judges this the most apparent meaning. Others, including Ibn Abbas in another report and al-Dahhak, say the angel covers that same distance in one day of our world, while Qatada divides it into five hundred years of descent and five hundred of ascent. Mujahid holds that God decrees the affairs of a thousand years in one day and then hands them to the angels. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi give several senses of the word for command, such as revelation, decree or worldly affairs. Some hold that this day is the Day of Resurrection, which the disbelievers find lasting fifty thousand years, a point some reconcile with the verse in the Ascending Ways. Ibn Abbas, asked about the two durations, declined to give a view, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab did the same. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi give further readings without settling the matter.

This verse describes God as the One who knows the unseen and the seen, the Mighty and the Merciful. The commentators explain that the word "that" refers to the Creator who governs the universe, whose acts were mentioned just before: the creation of the heavens and the earth and the management of affairs. Al-Tabari takes the unseen to be what escapes sight and what does not yet exist, and the seen to be what eyes perceive and what exists. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that some understood the unseen as the Hereafter and the seen as this world, while others took it as what is hidden from creatures and what they witness. For al-Tabari, "the Mighty" means the One whose punishment is severe toward those who disbelieve, and "the Merciful" the One who does not punish those who repent. The next verse, on the perfection of everything created, gives rise to several readings: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid understood it as making something firm and perfect, Qatada as making it beautiful, and Mujahid and Muqatil as giving each thing what it needs. The recitations differ over whether the lam of the word for creation is vowelled or not, and both are judged valid. The commentators say that man was first created from clay, in the person of Adam, and that his offspring came from a base drop of fluid, and that God then shaped him, breathed into him of His spirit, and gave him hearing, sight and hearts, though people are little thankful. As to the length of the day in which the matter ascends back to Him, opinions differ: al-Tabari, with Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, counts a thousand years between heaven and earth for the round trip, while Qatada links it to the Day of Judgement. All agree that the verse shows God's knowledge, power and mercy toward His creatures.

The commentators explain that this verse describes God as the one who made everything He created good, that is, perfect and firm, so that each creature was shaped according to wisdom and benefit, even though creatures differ in degrees of beauty. The verse then turns to the creation of man: God began the creation of the human being, Adam, the father of mankind, from clay, and then made his offspring from an extract, a lineage, of a despised fluid, which is the drop of semen. The commentators agree that the beginning of human creation refers to Adam, and that the despised water is the male seed.

The meaning of the word "ahsana" has been discussed in several ways. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean perfecting and making firm; others, as reported by al-Mawardi and al-Razi, take it to mean making everything beautiful. Al-Sudi and Muqatil explain that God taught each creature how to be created, or inspired each kind with what it needs, as al-Farra' put it. Some readers read "khalqahu" with a sukun and treated it as an apposition or a verbal noun, while al-Tabari preferred the sense of perfection and firmness in the reading with a fatha.

Several commentators note that the verse also carries a reminder of divine blessings. Ibn Kathir and others see creation, shaping, the breathing of the spirit, and the gift of hearing, sight and hearts as favours that call for gratitude, which explains the closing words "little is it that you give thanks". The details of the stages of creation are discussed by al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and others, but many limit themselves to the general statement of the verse.

This verse describes the creation of man and his offspring. The commentators explain that God began the creation of Adam from clay, then made his descendants come from an extract, a choice essence separated from the human, drawn from a base and worthless water, which is the seminal fluid. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain the word mahin as weak, and Mujahid also speaks of the weakness of the drop. Ibn 'Abbas adds that the sulala is the purest part of the water. All agree that the verse traces the stages of human creation, from its clay origin to its formation from the drop. Al-Zamakhshari explains that descendants are called nasl because they separate from the father, and that sulala takes its name from being drawn out of the human. Al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy understand the base water to be semen, while Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a hint that only a part of this water is used in forming the embryo. The commentators agree on the general meaning, which highlights God's power and wisdom, and on the fact that man comes from a humble origin before being honoured. They differ mainly on the details of the stages and the precise wording, and none of them settles the disagreement between the views.

This verse describes how God perfected the human being, breathed into him of His spirit, and gave him hearing, sight and hearts so that he might hear, see and understand. The commentators agree that the verse begins with Adam and then speaks of his descendants, with the address 'you' directed to the children of Adam. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the closing phrase to mean that people give only little thanks for these favours. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that this expression can also mean that there is no thanks at all. Al-Razi explains the order in which the faculties are mentioned: hearing comes first because a child hears before he sees, and then reasons. He also explains that hearing is mentioned in the singular because it is a single faculty over which the ear has no choice, whereas sight and the heart are in the plural because the eye and the heart have a degree of choice. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read the phrase 'of His spirit' as an honour, not as a part of God. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi share this reading. The next verse reports the disbelievers' question about resurrection once bodies have been scattered in the earth. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take 'dalalna' to mean 'we perished', while Ibn Kathir cites a reading attributed to Ali, 'sallalna', meaning 'we became rotten'. The question is understood as rhetorical denial of resurrection rather than a genuine inquiry.

The verse reports the objection of those who deny resurrection: after they have perished and become dust mixed with the earth, will they be created anew? Most commentators understand the verb 'dalalna' as perishing, dissolving, or being mingled with the soil; al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak take this line, and al-Tabari and al-Mawardi cite al-Akhtal's verse on water lost in milk. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi also give the sense of being buried, supported by a line of al-Nabigha that Qutrub cites. Some readings, attributed to Ali, Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, have 'salalna', meaning they became putrid, or a variant with a kasra. All agree the question is one of rejection rather than genuine inquiry. Al-Razi links the verse to the preceding points on prophethood and monotheism. According to al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, the phrase 'nay, they disbelieve in meeting their Lord' goes further than denying resurrection alone: they reject everything that awaits humans in the hereafter, including the encounter with God. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that the angel of death, named Azrael in tradition, takes the souls, and that all return to God for judgement.

This verse answers those who denied the Resurrection and asked, "When we have been lost in the earth, shall we truly be a new creation?" The plain meaning is that the Angel of Death, who has been entrusted with you, will take your souls when your terms end, and afterwards you will return to your Lord for reckoning and recompense. Commentators explain that "dalalna" means to be lost, to vanish, or to be mixed with the dust, and that their rejection of return in fact came from their denial of meeting God.

The commentators agree that "tawaffa" means to take the soul completely, leaving nothing behind, and that the Angel of Death acts by God's command. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold that the Angel of Death is a specific being, named Azrael in some reports, who has assistants among the angels. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that other verses attribute the taking of souls to God, and explain that the Angel carries it out as an intermediary. Al-Razi argues that the verse implies the survival of souls after death, and that the pure soul and the corrupt soul have different states. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the verse mainly concerns the Resurrection, with death mentioned to make the warning more vivid. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qasimi emphasise the theme of recompense.

Several works relate narrations about the Angel of Death, including the report that the earth is presented to him like a basin, and the story of his being watched by Ibn Kathir. Some commentators consider these reports weak or strange, while others present them without deciding their authenticity. Most do not choose between the differing views on the exact nature of the Angel and his assistants.

This passage describes the state of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection when they stand before their Lord. They will bow their heads in shame, humiliation and regret, saying: Our Lord, we have seen and heard; send us back so that we may act righteously, for we are now certain. The commentators agree that the answer to the conditional particle law is omitted, and that the sense is: you would see a dreadful and astonishing scene. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they now see and hear what they once denied, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi understand that they acknowledge the truth after it is too late. Regarding the word muqinun, al-Naqqash takes it to mean believing in the resurrection, whereas Yahya ibn Sallam takes it to mean believing in what Muhammad brought. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya report that God refutes them by saying that they would return to what they were forbidden if they were sent back. The commentators also differ on the sense of nisyan (forgetting) in what follows: Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as abandonment, and the image of tasting refers to feeling the punishment. On the next verse, al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain that God could have guided every soul by compulsion, but his word has been fulfilled: He will fill Hell with jinn and humans. Al-Zamakhshari reports the disagreement between the Sunnis and the Mu'tazilites on this point.

This passage of Surah As-Sajda describes the criminals on the Day of Judgement standing before their Lord with bowed heads, saying: "Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so send us back that we may do righteousness; we are now certain." The commentators read the bowed heads as shame, humiliation and regret, and "we have seen and heard" as seeing the truth of the threat and hearing the confirmation of the messengers. God's reply, "Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance," is interpreted in different ways. Al-Tabari and Qatada take it as a guidance by compulsion, such as a sign that would force belief. Al-Zamakhshari argues that compulsion contradicts responsibility, so God built the matter on free choice. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that God did not will to guide the disbelievers because He knew they would choose disbelief. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that God grants those He wills a subtle grace that brings them to faith. All agree that "the word is true from Me: I will fill Hell with jinn and men together" means the threat was decreed, and they connect it with the words spoken to Iblis. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and others identify the jinn as the jinn. Then they are told: "Taste because you forgot the meeting of this day." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Baghawi explain forgetting as abandonment and neglect of preparation. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see the punishment as corresponding to their own conduct. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir add that, if they were returned, they would go back to what they had been forbidden.

This passage describes the state of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection, heads bowed in shame before their Lord, as they say: Our Lord, we have now seen and heard, so send us back to act righteously, for we are now certain. The commentators agree that repentance at the moment of facing punishment does not benefit them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that God's words, 'Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance', mean that He could have guided them by compulsion, but they chose blindness over guidance, so the decree stands: He will fill Hell with jinn and humans. Ibn Kathir stresses that this decree is unalterable. As for 'Taste it because you forgot the meeting of this day', most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, take 'forgetting' to mean abandoning rather than involuntary lapse: they gave up belief in the Resurrection and preparation for it, so God treats them accordingly ('We have forgotten you', meaning We leave you to the punishment). Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see metaphor or a correspondence of treatment here. The commentators agree that the 'punishment of eternity' is a endless torment caused by disbelief, denial and sins. Opinions differ on what 'this' refers to: al-Razi offers three possibilities without deciding. Ibn Ashur and al-Sha'rawi read tasting as an image for feeling the punishment, and the reciprocity between deed and reward as a general rule.

This verse describes true believers: those who, when reminded of God's signs, fall down in prostration, glorify their Lord with His praise, and do not act arrogantly. Most commentators understand prostration as placing the forehead on the ground in reverence and fear of God, while Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean bowing (ruku'). Ibn Jurayj and Mujahid report that the verse concerned hypocrites who used to leave the mosque when the prayer was called; on this view the bowing is meant and the verse is Medinan, a view noted by Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari take the reminding to mean the recitation of the Quran and its admonitions. On glorification, some say it is the prayer performed at the Lord's command, others the words 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him', and Sufyan says it means praying in praise of the Lord. Yahya ibn Sallam explains not being arrogant as refusing to worship, while al-Naqqash understands it as refusing to prostrate as the people of Mecca did.

Regarding 'their sides forsake their beds', the majority, including al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Awza'i, take it to mean night prayer, which the Prophet ﷺ himself is reported to have explained as a man standing in prayer in the middle of the night. Anas, Qatada and 'Ikrima took it to mean the prayer between sunset and the night prayer, al-Hasan and 'Ata' the 'atama prayer, and Abu al-Darda' and al-Dahhak the dawn and night prayers in congregation. Calling on the Lord in fear and hope is understood as fear of His punishment and hope for His mercy, and spending includes obligatory and voluntary charity as well as provision for one's family.

On 'no soul knows what comfort of the eyes is hidden for them', the commentators cite the hadith qudsi about the rewards prepared for the righteous that no eye has seen. Hamza and Ya'qub read 'akhfi' in the present tense with God as subject, others in the passive. Ibn 'Abbas and others say the reward matches the deed, and several note that what is described is only approached through words, since the reality exceeds human imagination.

This verse describes believers whose sides withdraw from their beds at night, as they call on their Lord in fear and hope and spend from what He has provided. The commentators agree on the basic sense: the sides rise away from the places of sleep, and the supplication combines fear and longing. They differ, however, on which prayer is meant. The majority, including al-Hasan, Mujahid, Malik, al-Awza'i, Ibn Zayd and Abu al-Aliya, understand it as the voluntary night prayer, qiyam al-layl, supported by the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. Qatada and 'Ikrima take it to mean voluntary prayers between maghrib and 'isha', which Anas also reports, saying the verse was revealed about Ansar who prayed after maghrib. 'Ata and al-Hasan read it as the 'atama prayer, the night prayer after dusk, while Abu al-Darda', 'Ubada ibn al-Samit and al-Dahhak take it as 'isha' and fajr prayed in congregation. al-Tabari finds the night vigil the most apparent meaning and holds that any prayer in the night's hours is included. On almsgiving, some say it refers to the obligatory zakat, others to voluntary charity, and others to both; Ibn 'Atiyya considers the voluntary reading the more praiseworthy. The reports gathered by Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti describe the reward awaiting those who leave their beds to pray, which the following verse presents as a hidden joy that no soul knows.

This verse states that no soul knows what God has hidden for the believers described in the preceding verses, those who prostrate when reminded of God's signs, glorify their Lord without arrogance, rise from their beds in the night to pray, call on their Lord in fear and hope, and spend from what He has provided. This reward, which gladdens their eyes, is the recompense for their deeds. The commentators agree that it is a good unknown to all creatures, and they cite the hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." Al-Tabari reports that Abu Hurayra read "qurrat a'yun" in the plural. The readers differ over "uhfiya": Hamza and Ya'qub read it with a silent ya, God being the speaker, while most read it in the passive. As for the deeds meant, al-Hasan al-Basri says these people hid their deeds so God hid their reward; Ibn 'Abbas and others understand it as night prayer, while Anas and 'Ata' take it to mean the night prayer. Al-Razi explains that the coolness of the eye means a gaze that no longer seeks anything else. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the reward reflects both divine grace and justice, though the commentators do not decide between the two.

This verse states that the believer and the wrongdoer are not equal, and the interrogative form is a rhetorical denial of any equality between them before God, in this world and in the next. Commentators debate whether the terms refer to a general category or to two specific men. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' ibn Yasar report that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Walid ibn 'Uqba quarrelled, al-Walid boasting of his eloquence and courage, and 'Ali replying that he was a wrongdoer, whereupon the verse was revealed; al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas instead name 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that this version would make the verse Meccan, and doubt that al-Walid could be called a wrongdoer. Ibn Kathir stresses God's justice on the Day of Judgment.

The commentators agree on the fate of each group: the believers who do good receive the gardens of refuge as a welcome, while the wrongdoers have the Fire as their abode, and whenever they wish to leave it they are sent back in, and are told to taste the punishment of the Fire they denied. As for the lesser punishment mentioned next, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan take it to be the calamities of this world, Ibn Mas'ud the slaughter at Badr, al-Bara' and Mujahid the punishment of the grave, and 'Ikrima the prescribed penalties, while the greater punishment is that of the Hereafter. The phrase 'so that they may return' is taken by some to mean that they repent, and by others to mean that they wish to return.

This verse states that the believer who does righteous deeds is not equal before God to the depraved one who has departed from obedience to his Lord, and that each group receives a recompense suited to it. For those who believe and do good there are the Gardens of Refuge, where they will dwell, as a welcome gift (nuzul) in return for what they did, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain. Some commentators took the refuge to be one particular garden, where the souls of martyrs take shelter, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi relate from Ibn Abbas that it lies to the right of the Throne. The depraved, however, have the Fire as their refuge; whenever they try to leave it they are driven back, and they are told in rebuke: taste the punishment of the Fire that you used to deny. The scholars agree that fisq here means disbelief, and that the plural in the negation has a general application. They differ on the occasion of revelation: most report a quarrel between Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Walid ibn Uqba, while al-Tabari holds that the passage is Medinan and that al-Walid was not its subject, and al-Zamakhshari stresses that the general wording governs. On the lesser punishment the views vary: worldly calamities, the killing at Badr, famine, legal punishments, or the punishment of the grave, with the greater punishment being that of the Hereafter, and the purpose being that they might return to the truth. Turning away from God's signs after being reminded of them is regarded as the gravest wrong, and God will take vengeance on the criminals. Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith from Mu'adh ibn Jabal about three kinds of criminals, which he calls very rare.

This verse describes the fate of those who have committed fisq, that is, those who have departed from obedience to God through disbelief and disobedience. Their abode is the Fire, and whenever they wish to leave it they will be returned to it, and they will be told as a rebuke: taste the punishment of the Fire that you used to deny. The commentators broadly agree that fisq here means disbelief, since the denial at the end of the verse stands opposed to faith, as al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir note. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that the return happens when the flames throw them upward toward the top of the Fire and then they fall back to its bottom. Al-Zamakhshari suggests the phrase may also express the lasting nature of the punishment, and al-Razi observes that tasting the punishment increases their suffering, since they had denied it in this world. As for the lesser punishment mentioned next, which strikes the people of Mecca before the Hereafter, most commentators cite worldly calamities, famine, and killing at Badr, while others mention the prescribed penalties or the punishment of the grave. The greater punishment is that of the Hereafter. On the meaning of returning in the phrase perhaps they will return, Ibn Abbas and al-Baydawi take it as repentance from disbelief, while Ibrahim al-Nakha'i takes it as a return to the truth. Most commentators draw no legal ruling from this passage. The widely reported occasion of revelation concerns Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Walid ibn Uqba, though al-Zamakhshari reads the verse as general in scope.

God announces that He will make the defiant rebels taste a lesser punishment in this world before the greater punishment of the Hereafter, so that they may return to Him. The commentators agree that the greater punishment is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, but they differ on what the lesser punishment is. Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i take it to mean the calamities, illnesses and trials of this world, by which God tests His servants so that they repent. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan ibn 'Ali and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith take it to mean death by the sword at the battle of Badr, while Muqatil and Mujahid, in one report, mention the famine and years of hunger that struck the Quraysh in Mecca. Al-Tabari concludes that all of these fall under the lesser punishment, since God did not specify one kind over another. Ibn 'Abbas, in another report, understood it as the enforcement of legal penalties, and al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and Mujahid, in another report, as the punishment of the grave. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the phrasing "some of the lesser punishment" the idea that a portion of it remains after death. As for "that they may return", most explain it as repentance and abandoning disbelief, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as their wishing and seeking to return, and al-Razi notes that the hope expressed by "perhaps" is ascribed to the human rather than to God. Ibn 'Ashur observes that many converted after Badr and especially after the conquest of Mecca. The verse thus sits between the statement that the believer is not equal to the defiant sinner and the warning against those who turn away from God's signs after being reminded of them.

This verse states that there is no one more wrong-doing than the one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them with arrogance, and that God will take vengeance on the criminals. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qasimi and others take the criminals to be the polytheists or disbelievers, while al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Yazid ibn Rafi' apply the term to the Qadariyya, the people who deny predestination; Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi regard that reading as far-fetched. The hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal listing three kinds of criminals (one who raises a banner without right, one who disobeys his parents, one who walks with an oppressor to support him) is quoted by al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani and Ibn Kathir, who calls it very rare. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain that the word 'thumma' (then) expresses astonishment that one would turn away after such clarity, and they cite a line from the Hamasa. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi note that the text says 'the criminals' rather than 'him', so that the greatest wrongdoer receives the greatest share of vengeance. Ibn 'Ashur reads the sentence as an explanatory aside. Many commentators link the verse to the lesser punishment that God will make them taste before the greater one, so that they may return: some understand it as worldly calamities, hunger, or the deaths at Badr, others as the legal penalties or the punishment of the grave.

This verse states that God gave Moses the Book, the Torah, and tells the Prophet ﷺ not to be in doubt about meeting him, then says the Book was a guidance for the Children of Israel. The commentators differ on what the meeting refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir take it as the Prophet's meeting with Moses on the night of the Night Journey, citing the report that he saw Moses there. Al-Zajjaj and Mujahid understand it as Moses receiving the Book with acceptance, while al-Hasan reads it as consolation for the Prophet, since Moses too suffered rejection and harm. Others take it as a meeting on the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun in 'We made it a guidance' refers to Moses according to Qatada and to the Book according to al-Hasan. Most agree the guidance was for the Children of Israel in particular. The 'imams' among them are leaders in goodness who are followed, and most hold that this rank is reached through patience and certainty. Al-Tabari notes that the two readings of 'lamma' are close in meaning. On the nature of the patience, Sufyan and Qatada take it as patience toward worldly things, while others take it as patience in religion and against harm. The verse ends by saying that God will judge between the people on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they disputed, and Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di take this to mean that the disputes will be settled by God's truth.

This verse recalls that God gave Moses the Torah, made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, and then appointed from among them leaders in goodness who guided people by His command, because of their patience and their firm certainty in God's signs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari agree that the imams were leaders followed in good, and that the patience meant covers steadfastness in religion and under the harm of enemies, as well as turning away from worldly desires. Yaqin is firm conviction in God's signs. On who these imams were, Qatada, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi identify them as followers of the prophets or leaders of good, whereas al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan hold that they were the prophets themselves. The recitations differ on the word lamma: some read it as 'when' (lamma sabaru), others as 'because of' (lima sabaru). Al-Tabari considers both acceptable since they are close in meaning. On the pronoun in 'liqa'ihi', Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya report that it refers to the Prophet's meeting with Moses during the night journey, while al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj take it to refer to the Book or to the hardship Moses endured. The commentators conclude that God will judge between the disputing parties on the Day of Resurrection, and that the destruction of earlier peoples is a lesson for those who reflect.

This verse states that God alone will judge, on the Day of Resurrection, the disputes among people over matters of religion, the resurrection and reward, separating truth from falsehood: the people of truth will enter Paradise and the people of falsehood the Fire. The commentators agree on this basic meaning but differ on who is judged. Qatada and al-Naqqash take it to mean judgment between the prophets and their peoples, while Yahya ibn Sallam, followed by al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, takes it to mean judgment between believers and polytheists. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir extend it to the Children of Israel, the followers of the prophets and the innovators. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the blameworthy division is one born of desire, not the disagreement of scholars over legal details. Al-Sha'rawi observes that the detached pronoun 'He' expresses emphasis and exclusivity: no one but God will decide that day. In the verses that follow, the commentators explain that God directs the Meccans to reflect on the destroyed generations whose dwellings they pass, and on the water that revives barren land, as evidence of resurrection.

This passage of Surat al-Sajda states that God will judge between people on the Day of Resurrection over the religious matters they disputed. It then addresses the Meccan disbelievers with a rhetorical question of reproach: has it not become clear to them how many generations We destroyed before them, as they walk through their dwellings and see the remains with their own eyes? For most commentators, these ruins contain signs and lessons about God's power and the severity of His punishment against those who denied His messengers, so the listeners should hear and take warning. The exegetes agree that the verse carries rebuke and proof addressed to the polytheists, set within the context of belief in resurrection and prophethood. They differ on who is doing the walking: al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take it to be the Meccans passing through the dwellings of the destroyed peoples on their journeys to Syria, while others, such as al-Zajjaj, read it as describing the destroyed peoples themselves. On the grammatical subject of the verb meaning 'to guide' or 'make clear', grammarians disagree: al-Farra' allowed 'how many' to serve as subject, whereas al-Zajjaj and the Basran school rejected this; others supply the sense of guidance or make God the subject. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur hold that the repeated succession and disappearance of generations is a stronger proof than the sight of the remains of a single people. Few commentators draw any legal ruling from this verse; they confine themselves to its lesson and admonition.

This verse calls those who deny the resurrection to reflect on God's power to bring a dead land back to life: He drives water to it and brings forth crops on which their livestock and they themselves feed. The commentators differ on the meaning of "barren land" (al-ardh al-juruz). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi describe it as land with no vegetation at all, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi specify land whose growth has been cut off or grazed away, noting that salt flats incapable of growing anything are not so called. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid place it in Yemen or Abyan, al-Hasan between Yemen and Syria, and Ibn Kathir concludes that the phrase covers any land of this kind, though some mention Egypt.

The exegetes agree that the passage is an argument for resurrection: whoever revives the earth can revive the dead. Al-Razi explains that livestock are mentioned before people because the plant feeds the animals first and humans then eat from the animals. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi note variant readings, including "yaakulu" with a third-person singular and Ibn Mas'ud's "tubsirun".

On the "Day of Victory" mentioned in the next verse, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as the Day of Judgment or the day of decision between the two parties, and al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi lean the same way. Others link it to the battle of Badr or the conquest of Mecca, which Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Shawkani record without choosing between them. As for the command to turn away and wait, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that some scholars consider it abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others see no contradiction.

The verse reports the mockery of the disbelievers, who ask when this 'opening' (al-fath), meaning the decisive judgment that will separate the two sides, will come, if the believers are truthful. The commentators agree that the word primarily means judgment and decision, and that the question is sarcastic and impatient, a demand to hasten the punishment. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean the decisive verdict, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as both worldly punishment and the final judgment. The answer that follows has been understood in several ways. Mujahid, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir identify the 'day of the opening' as the Day of Resurrection, the day of judgment between reward and punishment. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi also allow a judgment in this world, such as Badr. Al-Farra', Ibn Qutayba and al-Zamakhshari take it to be the conquest of Mecca, an view Ibn Kathir rejects because the freed Meccans embraced Islam on that day, which the verse would then contradict. Al-Sudi thinks of Badr, and al-Zamakhshari replies that the meaning concerns those killed, whose faith no longer benefits them at the moment of death. All agree that faith is not accepted in the face of punishment and that no respite is granted then. As for the instruction to turn away and wait, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas consider it abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Baghawi reads the waiting as awaiting victory or punishment, and Ibn 'Ashur reads the turning away as withdrawing from disputation rather than from preaching. The general sense remains a call to patience for the Prophet, who should not preoccupy himself with these opponents, since they too are awaiting their fate.

This verse reports the mocking challenge of the disbelievers, who ask when this "victory", meaning the decisive judgment between the believers and themselves, will come. God tells His Prophet to answer that on that day faith will no longer benefit those who disbelieved, and they will not be granted respite to repent or make excuses. He then commands him to turn away from them and wait, for they too are waiting. The commentators agree in general that "fath" means judgment or decisive separation, but they differ on which day is meant. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Baydawi take it to be the Day of Resurrection or the day the punishment arrives. Al-Tabari adds that repentance was accepted both before and after the conquest of Mecca, which rules that event out. Al-Kalbi, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba identify it with the conquest of Mecca, but Ibn Kathir objects that the Freed Captives' Islam was accepted that day. Al-Sudi and one report from Ibn Abbas point to the Battle of Badr. Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi suggest that only the disbelievers killed in battle are meant, just as Pharaoh's faith did not save him from drowning. On the command to turn away, Ibn Abbas holds that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword, Qatada places it before the order to fight, and others say it was never abrogated. Al-Razi lists several readings of the waiting, whether for the enemies' ruin, for God's victory, or for their punishment. The common ground is that repentance is no longer accepted once the punishment is seen, and that the one who persists in denial is left to meet what he deserves.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from the polytheists who mockingly demanded the punishment, and to wait for what God will decide concerning them, for they too are waiting for what awaits them. The commentators broadly agree on the meaning: not to be drawn into their ridicule or their disputes. As for the waiting, some understand it as awaiting the victory promised to the Prophet, others as awaiting the punishment of the disbelievers. Al-Tabari holds that the disbelievers asked when the decisive judgment between them and the believers would come, the phrase referring to punishment or reward. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi follow this reading, while al-Kalbi and al-Farra' take the 'opening' to be the conquest of Mecca, al-Sudi the battle of Badr, and Mujahid and Qatada the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya reject the conquest of Mecca, since the Tulaqa' embraced Islam on that day. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note that 'fath' means victory or judgment, and that the divine reply avoids specifying the time. On abrogation, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sam'ani and Ibn Juzayy consider the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Qurtubi holds it is not, since turning away can coexist with the command to fight. The minority reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa' with a fatha, meaning 'awaited', is explained by al-Farra' as referring to the expected ruin of the disbelievers, while Abu Hatim prefers the kasra. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi conclude that the verse contains a veiled threat to the disbelievers and a promise of victory to the believers.
